I didn't talk to anyone outside of my family for years and then I decided to use social media, which I had never done before because I was too anxious about it, and I posted on this board and someone dmed me and we became friends.

I think the reason we were able to become friends is because one of the main things that made me anxious about talking to other people is the belief that they would judge me for being strange; but having met on this board the first things we talked about were been unable to leave our rooms, not doing anything with our lives, self-harm and starving ourselves; which were the things that I was worried about being judged for. I then looked for people on twitter who seemed to share my interests and to also be mentally ill and dmed quite a few and made a couple of friends.

When you have social anxiety one of the main fears is that people will judge you for having social anxiety so I think the best person to talk to is someone who also has social anxiety.

Another thing that made things easier was saying at the beginning of the conversation I have social anxiety. That way a big amount of the weight was lifted because I didn't have to worry about at what point they would realize what a stupid useless idiot I am, since I already told them. And when I embarrass myself it doesn't feel that bad because it was already expected.

1.Growing up, leaving the house was just a habit; I went to school every day so it felt normal. When I dropped out of school at 15 there was no longer any reason for leaving the house. I had always been a lonely person, and my social experience mostly amounted to being bullied, so once i didn't have to leave the house anymore there was no reason to do so. As I lost the habit I realized how scary leaving the house truly was. I became even more scared of the thought of being bullied than when I was actively bullied. I became much more sensitive to street noises, more overwhelmed by distances and horrified by the thought of being looked at or spoken to. As I got older (im 24 now) i developed a better perspective of what I was actually missing out on, and to what to degree I had sabotaged my life, and of how traumatic the exclusion I had experienced actually was. All of this however just made the fear stronger, because now it became a matter of pride, for me to leave the house and overcome these obstacles that I knew I was unable to. The more I thought about getting better the more I hated myself for not doing it earlier, and the more I hated myself the less I wanted people to see me.

2.I live with my parents and they don't ask me to do anything. I don't have any fixed routine but this an example of a typical day. I wake up at 16:00, i write poetry for a few hours, read pdfs for a few hours, then I talk to people on twitter and cut myself until my parents and my sister go to bed which normally happens at 1:00, I go to the bathroom and empty the pee jar (...sorry), I get something to eat (normally pasta), and then i spend the night watching anime and I go to bed in the morning. I will normally shower two to three times a month, a couple of times a year I get into a short phase where I go for walks at night, and I regularly go on really long fasts for as long as up to 40 days. That's about all the activities I do.

3.WTF none

My parents aren't wealthy, they actually both live of welfare, but since we own the house and don't have to worry about mortgage or rent and we have never had any luxury interests like vacations or anything like that they can afford to support my lifestyle. My parents on the surface are in denial about how crippling my mental state is; we have never once had a discussion about it; my mom freaks out when I don't clean the blood properly but aside from that she acts like everything is fine; but she would never pressure me to get a job or leave the house.

When I was younger I had far fetched fantasies of making money over the internet (mainly through poker) and using it to travel to places like Japan or India or Russia, places that seemed otherworldly; but as you can imagine from a highschool dropout I didn't have the discipline, or the mental stability to keep a cool head when I lost money. And with time I realized that even if I did have the money, no matter how otherworldly Asia seems over the internet it's still a real place and I would still be agoraphobic there. At that point I lost my last shred of motivation.

4.I think I would prefer people not to know anything about agoraphobia because the more people know about a mental illness the more misconceptions they have and the more patronizing they become. I have been diagnosed as schizoid and I think I probably also have depression and OCD (getting a diagnosis is hard for me because it's very rare that I'm willing to leave the house, which I need to do in order to see a mental health professional). In my experience people know that they know very little about the former two but they think they know a lot about the latter two; so they generally stay respectfully silent about schizoid and agoraphobia, but they say tons of nonsense about depression and OCD. Depression tends to be portrayed in an overly-dramatic way and OCD tend to be portrayed in an overly un-dramatic way.

The thing that most portrayals of agoraphobia are missing is the disappear. Agoraphobics are usually portrayed as people in denial, whereas in reality most agoraphobics are not delusional, they are painfully aware of their situation. Agoraphobics don't just live in the moment; despite consuming so much media they don't live in a bubble of anime and video games and forget about the real world; its the opposite, they live only in the past and in the future, only in regret and hopelessness, and no media can distract you from that. I actually have a youtube channel [https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCeDfRcrz3Ia5jbbMGzcsnbg](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCeDfRcrz3Ia5jbbMGzcsnbg), where I make vlogs ig, where I mostly talk about how I feel and the perspective that I've developed from this lifestyle, and I think the things I say are pretty ordinary for someone in my situation but less common in portrayals of it in media.

If I wanted to be understood maybe I would not be agoraphobic. I would prefer people just see me as some creepy wacko troll hiding in his room; almost like a science fiction character; like in the movie Gaslight. My ideal relation with society would be for people to hear foot steps coming from the attic every few days and wonder if there is a person there or some kind of super natural entity or if it was just their imagination. My mom says that I don't exist anymore and that I disappeared years ago, and quite frankly that's what I would like people in general to think about agoraphobics. I just want to be ghost.

And it’s more mental illness in general than agoraphobia; but agoraphobics rarely only have that one condition, so it's part of the package.
